notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00522.opp-gr: Section 1: the list of manuscript sigla and the running head printed in the middle of the Greek have been left out as page matter. Section 2: the words 'the same [god]' assume that τὸν αὐτὸν refers to the god of the altar, Mercy (Eleos); it could also be taken loosely of the altar (βωμός is masculine). Section 5: τῆς ὑποθέσεως, rendered 'your foundation', could also mean 'your policy' or 'your principle'. Section 6: Ἄπεμψε is read as Ἔπεμψε, 'sent'; the object 'to you' is understood. The sentence τὸ γὰρ <ἐμὲ> μόνον δηλοῦντος ἦν is awkward and the rendering is tentative; the transmitted αὐτα is read as αὐτῷ, 'with him'. Section 8: the Lacedaemonians' clause runs loosely, since τὰ τείχη κατηνέγκατε means literally 'you pulled down [your] walls'. Section 12: ὑέ is read as ὑπ’, 'by [me]'. The phrase on the Phocians is elliptical; '[were left]' is supplied, on the assumption that the rest had been lost through the men of false promises.

Sec. 14: the edition's supplement <γέμον> is kept in angle brackets. Sec. 17 (ref 16.2): ἐξῄτησε ... ζητῶν is awkwardly redundant and the verb may be corrupt; rendered once as 'sought'. Sec. 15: 'the ships' (τὰ πλοῖα) probably refers to a specific incident of ship seizure, which is not named. Sec. 22: μέχρις ἂν is taken as 'so long as', with the contrast developed in the next sentence. Sec. 26: the reference to 'the guardian of the grain convoys' renders ὁ τῆς σιτοπομπίας φύλαξ.

Section 27: the scanned ὡς τριον is read as ὡς πάτριον ("an ancestral custom"). Section 28: ἔν ἄρχωσιν is read as ἵν’ ἄρχωσιν; the sense "to gain power" is uncertain, and the reference may be to holding command or rule. Section 30: the words after <τὸν> are damaged. καὶ δορούμενον is not a Greek word and a supplement seems to be lost; δορυφορούμενον ("attended by a bodyguard") or ὀδυρόμενον ("lamenting") are possible, so the gap is marked [...]. Also in 30, the printed text repeats τῶν χαλεπαινόντων ("of those who are aggrieved") where sense requires something like τῶν λελυπηκότων ("of the offenders"); this is translated according to the required sense, and the repetition looks like a copying error. Section 31: ἐν τοῖς ἔμπροσθεν is obscure; it is taken as "as before", i.e. in its former standing. Section 34: ὁμοίας καθ’ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν πρεσβείας refers to embassies demanding their surrender, as with Demosthenes.

nodes.text: XXII.

Philip demanded the surrender of Demosthenes. Demosthenes took refuge at the Altar of Mercy. He was dragged away and handed over. And, released by Philip, he proposes among the Athenians that the altar be abolished.
Demosthenes.

Having suffered, men of Athens, the strangest things of anyone who has ever suffered, handed over by these men by whom I hoped to be saved, and saved by that man whom I had spent all my time grieving, I have come still loving my own country as before, for not even if I were to suffer things more terrible than these could I put an end to that, but with the intention of withdrawing from a political career that is perhaps irksome to you and dangerous to me.

Yet, though I have so resolved, I have come forward before you to speak on behalf of this one last thing alone: if you are persuaded by it, you will gain greatly in reputation, but if you do not accept it, you will keep secure for the city the great and abundant disgrace that has now come about. And this is that this altar here be abolished, which by what was done to me you have shown to be worthless.

Now, if those who claim to love you cared for what benefits the people, immediately after my surrender, which you carried out, lightly destroying your reverence for the altar, they would have spoken these words that you will now hear from me, and would have urged you to tear up the altar, on the ground that it is not right for you to honour the same [god] with sacrifices and to dishonour him by dragging away his suppliants. But since this has been neglected by these fine men who owe you great gratitude, because you have allowed them to do whatever they wish and to live with complete licence, and since the motion on this matter too had to be put forward by me, along with the many I have set out before, I shall, though without pleasure, go up to this platform, which received my long and continuous political service, but has brought me such a reward as you know, and I shall bring myself to address the people just this far, and to teach the city that it would be better off for abolishing the altar.

4. And yet, by Athena, even if all the seers had foretold that I would one day utter these things among the Athenians, and that Demosthenes would let fall such words, I would never have believed them when they said it. Why? Because such words, men of Athens, do not belong to my principles; those things belonged to others, not remembering the ancestors, not remembering their spirit, not imitating the fathers, and becoming different men, whereas I, quite the contrary, thought it right to look to them, to make them the pattern of one's life, and not to desert the post handed down.

And at some point, rebuking you, I, bold in everything, even said something of this sort: "You have departed, men of Athens, from your foundation," and I added your idleness in regard to military expeditions, for I saw that this part in particular had been neglected by the city, but I know of no occasion when I rebuked you over the honours paid to this altar as having been carelessly let slip. For I did not see anything of the kind happening with regard to it; on the contrary, although in other matters you had departed far from the ways of your ancestors, and had put the pleasure of the theatres ahead of concern for the Greeks, you strictly kept the laws concerning this [altar], knowing well that what brought the city glory was not so much being able to defeat its enemies on land and sea as being humane in disposition, being ready for pity, and counting Mercy among the gods.

6. How, then, have I come to the present speech? Philip sent [to you], wanting me from you, doing a thing to be expected, desiring to have in his power the man who stood opposed to him on your behalf, who had shut him out of many harbours, cities and places, and who would not let the people sleep. At such embassies coming to you I was wonderfully pained, but I also had something in them to take pleasure in. For this was surely clear testimony that I, above all those in the city, obstruct that man's desires. For [demanding] me alone was the mark of one showing that some work with him, others do not greatly trouble him, but Demosthenes is the one who owes the Macedonians a penalty for many great things.

So I reasoned with myself: "Demosthenes, you see the danger, and these men have come for your person. What, then, do you intend to do? You have an unstinting supply of arguments, since on this matter alone it is easy even for private citizens to say a great many and very just things, namely: 'Men of Athens, if you know that this has ever happened in this city, and someone can read out a decree according to which a citizen or foreigner or resident alien was handed over by you to enemies demanding him, then, though it is not good to follow bad precedents, let similar things be proposed and done now too, and let there be no help for those in danger. But if you have received from your fathers a law, confirmed by deed, that the right is not to be abandoned for any fear, do not hand me over now either.'

8. One could also mention the campaigns on behalf of those who had wronged you, some by sea and others by land, on the one hand the one on behalf of the Thebans to Haliartus, on the other the one on behalf of the Corinthians to Corinth, men who, though they owed you the heaviest penalties, were saved through your dangers. And far more brilliant than this is that the Lacedaemonians too met with the same treatment, the men through whom you were enslaved to thirty tyrants, deprived of your ships, and pulled down your walls. What, then, persuaded you to help such men? Nothing except knowing how to show mercy. For you leave off examining the suppliant's character and respect the bare [act] itself."

9. It was open to me, then, men of Athens, to say these things and more than these, and far more just ones, by examining what I have been towards you and towards the man demanding me. Why, then, did I not do this, or use my customary frankness towards the people, showing myself clean of every charge and worthy of being saved? Because even at that point I set great store by the interest of the city. For so that you might seem to send the embassy away empty-handed not because you were persuaded by the words of an orator but because you were prevented by fear of the gods, and might leave Philip no pretext for blaming the people, I set the altar against the arguments of the Macedonians, and I chose to put on a guise unworthy of myself and to sit at the sanctuary as a suppliant rather than give those who take his side [the chance] to reproach you.

With these reckonings, then, I ran to the altar, and at once many friends and relatives stood around me, all of them, men of Athens, weeping as they saw in what manner Demosthenes was escaping the hands of his enemies at Athens; but, as it turned out, I was not to escape even so. Such was the excess of my misfortune. For when the ambassadors had said what they had come for, and those who had often spoken in support of the Macedonians had spoken in support of them, while fear took away the voice of those who thought as I did, and someone reported to the assembly that Demosthenes of Paeania had taken refuge at the Altar of Mercy, you voted, men of Athens, that noble decree, that supplication was worthless, such protection a nonsense, the law concerning the altar a joke. For all this was contained in the order that I be dragged away and given to those who wished to take me.

The archers came running from the assembly, saw me sitting at the altar, wept first, and then announced what they would not have wished to: "Get up, Demosthenes, and follow the ambassadors in chains. For this is what the Athenians have resolved." I got up and obeyed, groaning much to myself over the altar that was no longer able to help its suppliants. They put me in chains and led me away with my head covered, for I could not bear to look at the statues of Harmodius and Aristogeiton, or at the council house, or at the Metroon, the places of my speeches and decrees.

The report of the supplication had run ahead, but was not yet fully believed, and some of the Thespians and Plataeans, through whose lands I was travelling, came up to me, lamenting and escorting me and doing all the other things that friends do, and finally asked whether this was really what came of the altar. I could not deny it, and I did not want to admit it. I heard something of the sort from old men of the Phocians too, for these alone [were left] in Phocis because of those men brilliant in their promises, by exposing whom I used to annoy those who were gladly deceived. The Thessalians, however, even mocked me, as men who had often been abused by me for the betrayal by which they betrayed the freedom of the Greeks.

I lamented together with my friends, and on seeing my enemies I shrank with shame, not as a wrongdoer would, for what wrong is there in conducting public affairs with courage? but because you were no longer the same. And when we came to Philip, who could relate what I heard in front of the palace from the mercenaries and the foot companions, who jeered and clapped and rejoiced as if they held Athens itself? But when Philip sat, solemn and in solemn state, brimming with joy and holding as a slave the man he had been unable to buy, and I was being led in through the bodyguards, he moved away from my person those who were pressing on me, and ordering me to look at him, he asked what harm I had suffered from his house that I had caused him so much vexation, stirring up the people, sending out forces, and urging them to plunder Macedonia.

But I, in no way cowering or humbled by the occasion, not as one who had been handed over but as an ambassador might, spoke with my customary frankness: "Everyone of sound mind, Philip, who does what is right loves his own country. And just as you live under arms in order to make your kingdom greater, so it is no wonder that an Athenian guards Athens. For you could not say this, at any rate, that I found the city thinking small and persuaded it to reach for a rank that did not belong to it; rather, you surely know, having learned of them, Marathon, Salamis, Artemisium, Plataea, Mycale, Cyprus, the boundaries that she set for the King, and I could go through countless things for you, Philip, being full of such narratives myself; and having inherited a speaker's platform <full> of solemn and noble deeds, I tried, I admit, not to fall short of the orators of old."

And about this great charge too, men of Athens, that I supposedly made war when it was possible to keep peace, I spoke and examined the facts, and by distinguishing the one defending himself from the one who starts a war, I was shown nowhere to be breaking the peace; instead Euboea, the Peloponnese, the ships, Megara, the Hellespont, small matters and greater, all of them cleared me of this reproach.

So I fell silent and expected whips and goads and fire and, finally, the slaughtering knife, but he paused briefly and said, "I release you and make you master of your journey wherever you wish; save yourself, and stay in my cities, if that is more pleasant, or go to Athens and recover your own home, if that is what you have in mind." And smiling, and looking at those present as he did so, he said, "And take care of the Altar of Mercy as well. For it is among you gentle people that it exists, while we are savage barbarians."

17. Now what the cause of this change was, and why, having in his hands the man he had been eager to take, he let him go, he himself would know exactly and could tell another; but to one making conjectures, men of Athens, many reasons might appear. For [it may be] that it was enough for him to have become master, and that he was overcome by justice, and that he pitied my fortune, and that he feared the obscurity of the future, and that he pursued a reputation for magnanimity by sparing an enemy, and that he sought to be thought more humane than the people of the Athenians. And we hear that he did something similar in the case of the daughters of Apollophanes too. For he released them to Satyrus the comic actor, although the girls' father had killed his brother.

18. Such, then, is what one might suppose about my rescue; but once freed and granted safety, I would not say that I deliberated where I should turn. And yet among many of the Greeks benefactions of mine were stored up, and they would gladly have given me a share of citizenship and land and other good things, but these things were not for a soul like mine, and I at once hurried home. So strong a love of my country is fused into me, and not even being handed over can put an end to it.

So I made my journey as far as possible unnoticed, so as not to be seen by the Greeks again or be forced to hear bitter words against you. For there were, there were those who compared the release with the handing over, Philip with the Athenians, the enemy with the citizens. And these things must now be said in many parts of Greece. For when both this and that are known, I suppose, it is natural that each side should receive the words it deserves. So that I might not meet many who remembered the altar, I went on, hiding myself as far as I could. Having arrived, then, I carry out this one political act, as I said, and propose in writing to overturn the altar that stands to no purpose.

20. "So do you dare," he says, "to expel from its customary honour an ancient and venerable altar that has brought the city a good reputation?" Am I the one doing this, men of Athens? Am I destroying a prevailing honour, I who by fleeing to it for refuge confirmed the law for it? This is pretence and the play of those who do not wish to seem to know that what has already been done in deed is now merely meeting with words. For who does not know that the altar was thrown away from that day on which it could no longer rescue its suppliant?

For come, what is the altar's honour? To save the wronged man who comes to it. What then? Was it enough to deliver me? How could it be? So the stone stands, but its privilege has ended, and it remains in appearance, while in truth it has been removed. For if you take away the reverence that altars have from the laws, the altar is gone, and it is what it was before it came to be regarded as an altar. And indeed the images of the gods are more revered than other figures because of their honours, but without these they are no better than the rest of the statues, or even than stones not yet carved.

No one before dared to touch those who fled there. No one heard me saying that this altar should be abolished. Its alliance has been abolished by what was done to me. Then let the altar not even be seen, so long as Athena is served at the Panathenaea, Demeter at the Mysteries, Pan with the torch race, and each of the other gods with the ancient rites.

Their altars stand for them rightly, but if their festivals and their other sacred rites were lost, it would be folly to preserve the altars. Now the festival of Mercy and its one service is that those who flee there should be saved, and when this is no longer so, what need is there of an altar? It is as if people took away a general's command and then saw fit to call him general. But the title is nothing apart from the deeds.

24. "What, then, shall we gain," he says, "by abolishing the altar?" You will escape, men of Athens, the present accusations that you incur by regarding Mercy as a god yet dragging away its suppliants. For this is the conduct of people who act against themselves and are at war with themselves, which I consider the greatest of reproaches. For not to revere those one does not think worthy of honours might earn a charge of ignorance, but to behave shamelessly toward what one places in the rank of gods falls nothing short of impiety.

So in abolishing it altogether lies not believing [it] a god, whereas in leaving the altar lies not shrinking from outraging even what you have thought worthy of altars. For see what happens. People will come to your city, they will see the altar, they will learn what happened. What do you want them to think about you? That the Athenians lie and cheat all mankind and lay ambushes for the unfortunate, and keep the Altar of Mercy as a hunting net, catching through hope of the altar those who could have saved themselves by flight?

For indeed, if no one who remembers my case will come to it, what would it even be kept for? But if people will come and profit and find a worthy saviour, what argument would you have about my being handed over? That, by Zeus, I am a most wicked man, the least deserving of humanity? Or not so very wicked, but useless, the man who shouted on behalf of the Olynthians, men of Athens, and served honestly as ambassador, and paid for choruses out of love of honour, and served as trierarch voluntarily, and ransomed prisoners, and helped give daughters in marriage? The man who pitied many, but has not met with pity? Who aided the navy with laws? Who increased the revenues? Who added to the alliance? The guardian of the grain convoys? The man proclaimed by the herald? The man crowned? Shall I name something better than these? The man whose surrender was demanded? Which of those who ever used the altar had these things to his credit? And they have been able to help me not at all. Having disregarded this man, then, will you pity another? And how is that not great madness?

27. "For it would have been necessary," he says, "to go to war if we had not done this." I could, for my part, have shown that it is an ancestral custom for you to go to war on behalf of such people, and, if I wished, I could have enumerated many struggles for which you delight in being praised in tragedies: on the one hand, the one on behalf of the Heraclidae against the whole Peloponnese, which Eurystheus, the man who gave trouble to Heracles himself, came leading; on the other, the one on behalf of the dead against the Thebans, men elated by victory and committing such outrages because of their present fortune. And yet, even if Heracles was revered, his children had done nothing, small or great, for you. Neither Adrastus himself nor his father Talaus had previously rendered any service to the city; these things came from mere pity and humanity and from being moved by those who supplicate.

What of Inaros the Libyan, what of Nicias the Cretan, what of Orestes the Thessalian? Did they not obtain ships and armies from here, to gain power, though they were foreigners and in no way connected with you? What would have been so terrible in doing something of your customary kind on behalf of an Athenian orator who had engaged in politics without deceit and was hated because of you, and by a single act freeing the people from such demands, teaching [him] that you do not know how to give such things?

This is what I would have said if it were clear that doing what was just would have brought war. As it is, I think that Philip would not have gone to such a pitch of absurdity as to make the people's reverence toward the divine a pretext for war. For what accusation could he even have sent? "You do wrong, men of Athens, because you do not fear me more than the gods, nor court my favour above your altars"?

But he would never have uttered so insane a statement, since he saw two penalties resulting from it: the one, to incur laughter among mankind; the other, to draw upon himself as harsh adversaries the outraged gods, who he knew would come with us against him in such a war. No, that man, who knows how to handle affairs, is not so senseless or foolish as to choose to seem deranged and to stir up the higher powers against himself. It would have been enough for him that the man [...] and great among you, and great among the other Greeks, was being saved by pity and tears and the suppliants' branch. For the anger of those who are aggrieved at those who have offended them is dissolved by the misfortune of the offenders.

Let what he has now done be your proof. For once he had seized me and held me and saw me, and had the power to throw me down a cliff, to cut me to pieces, and to treat me however he wished, he fixed his eyes on me, reflected on something to himself, and released me. I think he would have done this in response to the supplication too, if someone had reported it to him. For what more would he have sought than his enemy's defeat? In short, the argument from war and fear gives a reason for the handing over, but it is no proof for the altar's remaining as before.

32. Now we must not inquire what persuaded [you] to neglect the honour [due to it], but whether it is not advantageous to have obliterated once and for all this thing of no worth. Why, then, do you delay, men of Athens? Why do you not rush at it with all speed? Why do you not kick it over? Or rather, why do you not sink it in the sea? Whose hands should do the work? Those which dragged my body from the altar and handed it over to my enemies. Or rather, let it be the common work of all of you. You all voted; all of you, tear it up, or, if you like, let some tear it up and others urge them on.

Follow your own ways, since you do not follow those of your ancestors, who drove out the slayers of those who had seized the Acropolis with Cylon, considering them polluted and sinners against Athena. And yet those who brought a tyrant upon the laws had wronged the city more gravely, but nevertheless they thought that the gods were sufficient for the safety even of those who dared such things.

34. At that time, then, it was reasonable that no such proposal was moved, since the altars were honoured; but now why do you spare stones whose strength you have wiped out? Why do you groan, Hyperides and Polyeuctus and Lycurgus and all you who imitate my political career? I am not depriving you of a refuge, no. Rather, I do not allow you to be deceived by empty hopes. For who will stand by you, when he did not take the part of Demosthenes? Who will pity you, when he felt no shame before my labours? Who will give back to the altar in your dangers the strength that he took from it in mine? If, then, you expect similar embassies against yourselves, you seem to me to show good sense, and it is time for you to seek another means of escape.

As for me, I have found how I may be saved. Farewell to this place, once dearest to me, in which I used to advise the people; farewell to the council house and preliminary decrees and decrees and embassies and hardships that benefit everyone else but penalise the speaker. And yet Philip did not order this, at any rate, but I am being taught by my sufferings to be silent. You, however, stay at your post, if you see fit, but look around now for another harbour, since that of the altar, at any rate, has been closed. But if ever the Athenians become humane, and show again that they have pity in their nature, and renew mercy by their deeds, there will be someone to propose that the altar be set up again.
